prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Here take my picture; though I bid farewell Thine, in my heart, where my soul dwells, shall dwell. 'Tis like me now, but I dead, 'twill be more When we are shadows both, than 'twas before. When weather-beaten I come back, my hand Perhaps with rude oars torn, or sun beams tann'd, My face and breast of haircloth, and my head With care's rash sudden storms being o'erspread, My body'a sack of bones, broken within, And powder's blue stains scatter'd on my skin; If rival fools tax thee to'have lov'd a man So foul and coarse as, oh, I may seem then, This shall say what I was, and thou shalt say, "Do his hurts reach me? doth my worth decay? Or do they reach his judging mind, that he Should now love less, what he did love to see? That which in him was fair and delicate, Was but the milk which in love's childish state Did nurse it; who now is grown strong enough To feed on that, which to disus'd tastes seems tough."

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker gives his beloved a picture of himself as a farewell keepsake.
- He says the picture will preserve his former appearance even if he later returns changed by hardship.
- The speaker imagines coming back wounded, weathered, aged, and physically altered.
- He anticipates that others may mock his beloved for loving someone who has become rough and unattractive.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Here, Thine, Tis

outputs.L1:
Here, take my portrait. Though I bid you farewell, you shall dwell in my heart, where my very soul resides. It resembles me now; yet, when I am dead, it will resemble me even more than it does today, when we both have become but shadows.

When I return weather-beaten, my hands perhaps torn by rough oars or darkened by the sun’s rays; when my face and breast are coarse as haircloth, and my head is overtaken by sudden storms of care; when my body is reduced to a sack of bones, broken within, and blue stains of powder are scattered across my skin—if rival fools accuse you of having loved a man so foul and coarse as I may then appear, this image will bear witness to what I once was.

And you shall say: “Do his wounds diminish me? Does my worth decay because of them? Or do they reach his discerning mind so that he should love less what he once loved to behold? That which was fair and delicate in him was only the milk that nourished love in its childhood. Now love has grown strong enough to feed upon what, to unaccustomed tastes, may seem harsh.”
outputs.L2:
Take this portrait of me. Although I am saying goodbye, the image—yours—will remain with you in your heart, where your deepest self resides. It resembles me now, but when I am dead, and when both of us are only shadows, it will resemble me even more than it does today.

If I return battered by storms, my hands perhaps torn by rough oars or darkened by the sun, my face and chest rough as haircloth, my head suddenly covered over by the violent tempests of care, my body reduced to a bag of bones and damaged within, with blue stains of gunpowder scattered across my skin—then, if jealous fools accuse you of having loved a man who seems so ugly and coarse as I may appear, this picture will show what I once was.

And you will answer: “Do his wounds diminish me? Does my value fade because of them? Or do they damage his ability to judge, so that he should now love less what he once loved to look upon? The beauty and delicacy that were in him were only the milk that fed love while it was still young. Now love has grown strong enough to live on what seems hard and unappealing to tastes that are no longer accustomed to it.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents his beloved with a picture of himself as a farewell keepsake, something she can hold onto while he is away. This image is meant to preserve the memory of how he looks at the moment of parting, before time, suffering, or hardship have had the chance to alter him. Even if he returns greatly changed, the picture will remain as a record of his former appearance.

He imagines the possibility that, when he comes back, he may no longer look like the man she once knew. His body may be wounded, his face weathered, his youth diminished, and his appearance marked by age and hardship. The speaker seems aware that experience can leave visible scars, transforming a person both physically and emotionally.

He also anticipates that others may judge or mock his beloved for continuing to love him if he becomes rough, unattractive, or physically damaged. They may wonder why she remains faithful to someone whose outward beauty has faded. However, the speaker suggests that her love is not shallow or dependent on appearances. Instead, her affection is mature and steadfast, capable of valuing his inner self beyond external beauty. The picture, therefore, becomes more than a simple portrait: it is a symbol of memory, loyalty, and a love strong enough to survive change.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the anxiety that love may weaken when the beloved is separated from the speaker and can no longer see him as he once was. Aware that time, illness, grief, and absence can alter the body, the speaker leaves behind his portrait as a reminder of his younger and more attractive self. The image becomes a substitute for his presence, preserving the version of him that his lover first knew and loved. At the same time, however, the poem questions whether love should depend so heavily on physical appearance.

As the poem develops, it suggests that genuine love must move beyond the surface of youth and beauty. The portrait may recall the speaker’s former self, but it cannot be the true foundation of affection. Bodies change, faces age, and suffering may leave visible marks, yet these changes should not destroy a faithful bond. The speaker’s concern about being forgotten or rejected reveals a deeper fear: that love based only on beauty is fragile and temporary.

Ultimately, the poem affirms a more mature idea of love. True devotion should survive separation, physical decline, and hardship. Rather than being tied to an idealized image, love should recognize and remain loyal to the whole person, even when that person is altered by time or pain. In this way, the poem presents love as something stronger than appearances: it may begin with attraction, but it proves itself through constancy, endurance, and faithfulness beyond youth and beauty.
outputs.L5:
Here is a small poetic text using the keywords **Here**, **Thine**, and **Tis**:

---

**Here**, beneath the quiet sky, where the evening light fades softly into gold, I stand and remember the promises once spoken. The wind carries whispers through the trees, gentle as a forgotten song, and every shadow seems to hold a memory.

**Thine** was the voice that brought comfort in sorrow, thine the smile that made even the darkest road feel bright. Though time may pass and seasons change, the heart keeps what it truly loves, guarded like a flame against the night.

**Tis** not distance that weakens devotion, nor silence that erases hope. For where love has once taken root, it blooms beyond sight, beyond time, beyond the reach of ordinary things. Here, in this still moment, I know that some bonds are never truly broken.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Renaissance-style love poem in the voice of John Donne about giving a portrait to a beloved before leaving for war.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Picture Sent Before the Wars**

Receive this shadow, love, before I go,  
This little night wherein my day is drawn;  
For when the trumpets chide the cocks to crow,  
And steel makes haste to out-salute the dawn,  
Here shall I stay, though hence my body run,  
A lesser me, yet truer than the sun.

Look not that colours can my heart comprise,  
Or that dull oils should counterfeit my fire;  
The painter stole but treaties from mine eyes,  
And left unsacked the kingdom of desire.  
Yet if thy sight can breathe, thy tears can give  
A soul to this, and bid the dead thing live.

Think, when thou seest my hand upon my breast,  
It keeps an oath there, not a wound, for thee;  
And though in camps my troubled limbs find rest  
On earth less soft than thy remembered knee,  
My heart, encamped within this frame, shall prove  
No rebel drum can beat it from thy love.

If cannon tear the air wherein I pray,  
If hostile iron search my yielding side,  
This face shall make thee know I went away  
Not from thy love, but for it—armed with pride.  
For he that fights where honour bids him stand  
Doth still march homeward, led by thy command.

Then hang me near thy glass; and when thine eye  
Consults with beauty at the break of day,  
Let this poor painted pilgrim standing by  
Confess he worships where thy graces stay.  
So shall my image, blessed by looking on,  
Be more myself than I, when I am gone.

And if black news should fly before my breath,  
And say the field hath made my pillow red,  
Believe not wholly that report of death,  
Whilst this my second life looks up instead.  
For lovers in their pictures do not die:  
They change but rooms, and lodge within the eye.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3
